traveler: Jacob Boehme (Jakob Böhme), the shoemaker of Görlitz
title: The Pewter Dish and the Writing Ban: a Lusatian Shoemaker Describes the Being of God
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Alt Seidenberg and the Bench at Seidenberg

stops.name: Alt Seidenberg, the fourth child of a landholding peasant
stops.date_confidence: day and month given by en.wikipedia; some accounts give only the year 1575. Julian reckoning, retained in Lutheran Lusatia until 1700.
stops.campa: In the village of Alt Seidenberg, a few hours' walk from Görlitz in Upper Lusatia, a fourth child is born to the Lutheran peasant George Wissen and his wife. The family holds its own land, and the land is held of the Bohemian crown; the parish answers to Wittenberg. English Wikipedia gives the fourth of five children and the twenty-fourth of April; other accounts give only the year. The boy is called Jacob, and the trade he will be given is the one a frail farm child gets when he cannot follow the plough.
suggested_refs: The village of Alt Seidenberg, now Stary Zawidów in Poland, birthplace of Jakob Böhme

stops.name: Alt Seidenberg, the hollow in the hill
stops.date_confidence: legend, undated; earliest carrier is Franckenberg's Bericht of 1651, twenty-seven years after the death. The hill is not identified in any source; the later local attribution to the Landeskrone is geographically impossible, since that hill stands about 20 km away at Görlitz, and its coordinate is refused here. The stop is placed at the village and the date is a placeholder in boyhood.
stops.campa: A herdboy on his father's land follows a path he has not seen before up the hill above the village and comes on an opening in the rock. Inside stands a vessel of red gold. He takes fright and runs, touching nothing, and afterward the way back cannot be found. Abraham von Franckenberg sets the story down in 1651 and every later life repeats it. Local tradition names the Landeskrone as the hill; the Landeskrone stands twenty kilometres off, at Görlitz, and no village boy herded his father's animals there.
suggested_refs: Abraham von Franckenberg, Bericht von Jacob Böhmens Leben und Schriften (1651), source of both boyhood legends
sources: Franckenberg 1651, as transmitted by Durand Hotham (1654) and Stoudt (1957)
German Wikipedia, 'Landeskrone' (checked: contains no Böhme material)

stops.name: Seidenberg, apprenticed to the shoemaker
stops.date_confidence: about his fourteenth year, c. 1589; no month or day recorded
stops.campa: About his fourteenth year the boy is sent down from the village to the town, to a master shoemaker's bench in Seidenberg. He is too weak for field work and there is a trade for such children. He gets a village education and nothing further: no Latin school, no university, no patron. What he will later know of Scripture, of Paracelsus, of alchemy and of Kabbalistic material he takes from books lent and conversations overheard, in a language the learned of his century do not write philosophy in.
suggested_refs: The shoemakers' craft of Seidenberg, now Zawidów, where Böhme served his apprenticeship

stops.name: Seidenberg, the stranger who buys a pair of shoes
stops.date_confidence: legend, undated within the apprenticeship c. 1589-1592; Franckenberg 1651, carried into English by Hotham 1654 and still printed by Stoudt in 1957. No document of the period mentions it.
stops.campa: Left alone to mind the shop, the apprentice sells a pair of shoes to a stranger who pays a price no one would pay. The man goes out, then calls him into the street by his own name and tells him he will be small in the eyes of the world and great before God, and to hold fast to the Scriptures. Then he is gone, and cannot be found again. Franckenberg records it in 1651; Durand Hotham carries it into English in 1654; Stoudt still prints it in 1957. Nothing written in the 1590s mentions any of it.
suggested_refs: Durand Hotham, The Life of Jacob Behmen (1654), first English transmission of the Franckenberg legends
sources: Franckenberg 1651, via Hotham 1654 and Stoudt, Jacob Boehme: His Life and Thought (1957)

stops.name: Seidenberg, departure on the Wanderschaft
stops.date_confidence: c. 1592 per en.wikipedia; the years and the route are a stated gap
stops.campa: His apprenticeship finished, he leaves Seidenberg on the Wanderschaft the craft requires of every journeyman. Where he goes is not known. English Wikipedia says plainly that it is unknown just how far he went, and no early life names a single town of these years. Later readers have wanted Prague in them, or the Silesian mining country, or a Schwenkfelder household; nothing in the record supplies any of it. Two years, or three, or four, go unrecorded. He leaves Seidenberg at about seventeen and next appears in a document at Görlitz, a grown tradesman.
suggested_refs: The journeyman years, c. 1592-1594, for which no itinerary survives

stops.name: Görlitz, the journeyman stops travelling
stops.date_confidence: disputed and NOT resolved: en.wikipedia's chronology implies a return around 1592, de.wikipedia states '1594 ließ er sich in Görlitz nieder'. Tagged as reconstruction; 1594 used for placement only.
stops.campa: The journeyman comes back into the Neisse valley and stops at Görlitz, a rich cloth and dyeing town of the Bohemian crown, with its Latin school, its six churches and a council that answers to Prague. Forty-four licensed shoemakers' stalls stand on the Untermarkt under the arcades. He will spend the rest of his life inside a square kilometre of this town, and the cosmology he writes will be built from the only materials to hand: sulphur, salt and mercury, fire, the bitter and the sweet, a dyer's words and a shoemaker's.
suggested_refs: The Untermarkt of Görlitz and its forty-four licensed Schuhbänke

stops.name: Görlitz, enrolled a citizen at the Rathaus
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by de.wikipedia
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of April he is enrolled a citizen of Görlitz. Citizenship is the condition of everything else: no man may hold his own workshop or a stall on the Untermarkt without it. The town clerk writes the name of a peasant's son from a village across the hills into the register of a Bohemian free town. From this day he is a burgher, taxed, sworn and answerable to the council, and it is this same council that will one day sit and order him to leave.
suggested_refs: The Görlitz Rathaus at Untermarkt 6-8, where the citizens' register was kept

stops.name: Görlitz, the Schuhbank bought for two hundred and forty marks
stops.date_confidence: attested year; de.wikipedia associates the purchase with the citizenship of 24 April 1599
stops.campa: He buys one of the forty-four licensed shoemakers' stalls on the Untermarkt for two hundred and forty Görlitz marks and is admitted a master of the craft. It is a large sum and a settled life. For fourteen years he sits under the arcade cutting and stitching, a master with apprentices under him, and the townsmen who buy his shoes know him as a quiet tradesman of no particular learning. He is twenty-four when he buys the stall and thirty-eight when he sells it, and no writing of his from those years survives.
suggested_refs: The licensed shoemaker's stall on the Untermarkt, held by Böhme from 1599 to 1613

stops.name: Görlitz, the parish of St. Peter und Paul and the marriage to Katharina Kuntzschmann
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day not given in any source consulted. The venue is inferred and downgraded: St. Peter und Paul is the documented parish of both Böhme and Gregor Richter, but no source states that the wedding took place in it.
stops.campa: He marries Katharina, daughter of the Görlitz butcher Hans Kuntzschmann, and the couple keep house in the parish of St. Peter und Paul above the river. The children come between 1600 and 1611. German Wikipedia counts four sons; the New World Encyclopedia says four children; only English Wikipedia gives four sons and two daughters. The Oberpfarrer of this parish from 1606 is Gregorius Richter, who will preach at this family for eighteen years and denounce the husband from this pulpit.
suggested_refs: The Pfarrkirche St. Peter und Paul, Görlitz, parish of Jakob Böhme and of Gregorius Richter
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Pfarrkirche St. Peter und Paul (Görlitz)'

stops.name: Görlitz, the sun in the pewter dish
stops.date_confidence: year attested by en.wikipedia and the New World Encyclopedia; no day. Coordinates approximate the documented Prager Straße house, now ul. Daszyńskiego 12 in Zgorzelec on the east bank; the pool's 51.1524, 14.9865 corresponds to no documented Böhme address and is refused.
stops.campa: Sunlight strikes the burnished pewter of a dish in his own room and he cannot look away. What follows he describes afterward as an opening: the inward structure of the world, the relation of God to man, the ground of good and of evil. He walks out into the fields to shake it off and finds the grass and the herbs still legible. He says nothing publicly for twelve years and goes on making shoes. The house of these years stands on the east bank of the Neisse, on what was then the Prager Straße.
stops.quote: And then, when I had wholly hazarded my life upon what I was doing, my whole spirit seemed to me suddenly to break through the gates of hell, and to be taken up into the arms and the heart of God.
stops.quote_source: Jacob Boehme, Aurora ch. 19, quoted in Alexander Whyte, Jacob Behmen: An Appreciation (1895), p. 12
suggested_refs: The Jakob-Böhme-Haus, ul. Daszyńskiego 12 (former Prager Straße), Zgorzelec

stops.name: Outside the walls of Görlitz, the second illumination
stops.date_confidence: year attested by en.wikipedia. Content corrected: en.wikipedia describes the 1610 vision as concerning the unity of the cosmos and a special vocation received from God; the impulse to write is dated separately to 1612. The site outside the walls is unlocated and the coordinate is approximate open ground.
stops.campa: Ten years after the dish, in open ground outside the town wall, the thing returns and is larger. English Wikipedia has him understanding the unity of the cosmos and receiving a vocation from God. He is thirty-five, a master shoemaker with four sons and no learning, and what he now believes himself charged with is the description of the being of God. Two more years pass before he takes up a pen. The ground outside the wall is named in no source, and the pin here is a guess.
stops.quote: The gate of the Divine Mystery was sometimes so opened to me that in one quarter of an hour I saw and knew more than if I had been many years together at a university.
stops.quote_source: Jacob Boehme, quoted in Alexander Whyte, Jacob Behmen: An Appreciation (1895); Whyte names no treatise
suggested_refs: The open ground outside the Görlitz walls, site of the 1610 vision, unlocated in the sources

stops.name: Görlitz, the house on the Töpferberg
stops.date_confidence: purchase year attested by en.wikipedia; the address is unresolved. de.wikipedia's Böhme article names a Töpferberg purchase in 1599 and a Prager Straße residency 'from 1590', while its Zgorzelec article gives 1599-1610 for the same house, which fits; the 1590 appears to be an error in a photo caption. Recorded, not adjudicated.
stops.campa: The same year he buys a house in Görlitz. German Wikipedia records a purchase on the Töpferberg; a photograph caption in the same article dates his residence at Prager Straße 12 from 1590, which cannot stand against a settlement in 1594, and the article on Zgorzelec gives 1599 to 1610 for the same house, which fits. The buildings are all inside the same small town. A man who has just been told he must describe the being of God begins by moving his family, his lasts and his knives.
suggested_refs: The Töpferberg purchase of the de.wikipedia account, and the Prager Straße house at ul. Daszyńskiego 12

stops.name: Görlitz, the Aurora begun
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia dates the commencement to 1612, twelve years after the vision of 1600; the New World Encyclopedia dates the completion to about 1612. The start and finish boundary is not fixed by any source consulted.
stops.campa: Twelve years after the dish he begins to write, in a German nobody has written philosophy in, for no reader, with no thought of a press. He calls it Morgenröte im Aufgang, the dawn coming up, and what he leaves is unfinished. Sulphur, mercury and salt, the seven qualities, the astringent, the bitter and the sweet, the wheel of nature turning against itself: a vocabulary out of the alchemists and the dyers' shops, put to work on the interior life of God. He writes it, he says, as a memorandum for himself.
stops.quote: I am not come to this meaning, or to this work and knowledge through my own reason or through my own will and purpose; neither have I sought this knowledge, nor so much as to know anything concerning it. I sought only for the heart of God, therein to hide myself.
stops.quote_source: Jacob Boehme, Aurora, English translation of 1764, p. 237, quoted in Evelyn Underhill, Mysticism (1911), Part 1 ch. IV
suggested_refs: Aurora, oder Morgenröte im Aufgang, begun 1612 and left unfinished

stops.name: Görlitz, Karl Ender von Sercha copies the manuscript
stops.date_confidence: 1612, at the outset of the affair. The pool's geography lens dated this copying to the 'early 1620s', conflating it with the later circle of noble patrons; that dating is refused. de.wikipedia names Karl Ender von Sercha, en.wikipedia calls him Karl von Ender.
stops.campa: A nobleman of the district, Karl Ender von Sercha, gets hold of the manuscript and has copies made. German Wikipedia names him the copyist; English Wikipedia calls him Karl von Ender. The book written for no reader is now in circulation in a town of ten thousand people, passing between merchants, physicians and gentry, in the decade when the Rosicrucian manifestos are about to be printed a few hundred miles west and every Lutheran consistory in the empire is watching for enthusiasm.
suggested_refs: The manuscript copies of the Aurora made for Karl Ender von Sercha, 1612

stops.name: Görlitz, Gregorius Richter denounces the book from the pulpit
stops.date_confidence: disputed and NOT resolved: de.wikipedia dates the resulting arrest and Schreibverbot to 1612; en.wikipedia gives no year at all for the pulpit attack; the research pool asserted 1613 with nothing behind it. 1612 is used for placement and the conflict is left standing.
stops.campa: Gregorius Richter, Oberpfarrer of St. Peter und Paul since 1606, reads what his own parishioner has written and denounces it from the pulpit as heresy and enthusiasm, with the shoemaker sitting in the church. A print by Joseph Mulder of 1686 shows the pastor throwing a slipper at Böhme's head, and the tradition has Böhme picking it up, handing it back and wishing him every blessing. Whether that happened, or was made to have happened afterward, the sources do not settle.
stops.quote: Some men will mock me, and will tell me to stick to my proper trade, and not trouble my mind with philosophy and theology.
stops.quote_source: Jacob Boehme, quoted in Alexander Whyte, Jacob Behmen: An Appreciation (1895), p. 12; treatise of origin not given
suggested_refs: Joseph Mulder's 1686 illustration of the slipper anecdote

stops.name: Görlitz, the arrest and the Schreibverbot
stops.date_confidence: de.wikipedia: 'Daraufhin wurde Böhme kurzzeitig arrestiert und im Jahr 1612 mit einem Schreibverbot belegt.' Agent corrected: en.wikipedia attributes the exile threat to Richter personally, not to the town council, whose only recorded summons is 26 March 1624.
stops.campa: On the pastor's complaint he is briefly arrested and put under a writing ban. English Wikipedia has Richter himself threatening exile if the work continues; the only summons before the town council that it records falls twelve years later. German Wikipedia gives the arrest and the Schreibverbot to 1612. He hands over the Aurora manuscript, or it is taken from him, and he obeys. For five years or six the man who believes he was called by God to describe creation makes shoes and says nothing.
suggested_refs: The Görlitz Schreibverbot of 1612, the deliberate hole in the corpus

stops.name: Görlitz, the stall sold and the glove trade taken up
stops.date_confidence: attested year, en.wikipedia and de.wikipedia; no month
stops.campa: He sells the shoemaker's stall and gives up the craft, and takes to selling woollen gloves and yarn instead. It is the trade of a man who travels: gloves are light, yarn is light, and a merchant of small goods has reason to be on the roads that a master with a fixed bench under the arcade does not. He is forbidden to write. No one has forbidden him to go anywhere, and the new trade puts him regularly on the Prague road for the eleven years that are left to him.
suggested_refs: The Görlitz glove and yarn trade, Böhme's occupation from 1613

stops.name: Prague, the glove merchant on the Bohemian road
stops.date_confidence: attested as a recurring pattern, not as a dated journey: en.wikipedia says the trade 'caused him to regularly visit Prague to sell his wares'. No street, market, host or single visit is documented. The coordinate is the corpus canonical Prague pin, inherited byte-identical from giordano_bruno, kircher, steiner and hegel, not a documented Böhme address.
stops.campa: The glove trade takes him to Prague, capital of the crown his own town belongs to, again and again for the rest of his life. Böhme comes to sell yarn and gloves, a Lusatian tradesman moving through an imperial capital on ordinary business, and nothing in the record suggests he ever steps outside that business while he is there. What he carries home from the Bohemian book stalls is nowhere recorded, and no source names a street, a market or a host, only the trade itself and the years it repeats.
suggested_refs: The Prague of Rudolf II's successors, market of Böhme's glove and yarn trade

stops.name: Görlitz, the years of silence
stops.date_confidence: disputed length, NOT resolved: Wikipedia's chronology implies silence until roughly 1618-1619; the New World Encyclopedia says about five years. Broadly consistent, endpoints not identical. 1615 is a midpoint placeholder, not a documented date.
stops.campa: Five years, or six, in which he writes nothing. He is in his forties, selling gloves, going to church weekly to hear the man who broke his book preach, keeping a wife and four sons. What the ban costs him he does not say directly, but in a small treatise on the four temperaments he says he knows melancholy from the inside and has lodged in it all his days. Nothing survives from these years. The hole was made on purpose, and English Wikipedia puts the threat that made it on Richter personally rather than on the council.
stops.quote: O hear me! for I know well myself what melancholy is! I also have lodged all my days in the melancholy inn!
stops.quote_source: Jacob Boehme, Of the Four Complexions, quoted in Alexander Whyte, Jacob Behmen: An Appreciation (1895)
suggested_refs: Of the Four Complexions, Böhme's treatise on temperament and melancholy
sources: Alexander Whyte, Jacob Behmen: An Appreciation (1895)

stops.name: Görlitz, the silence broken
stops.date_confidence: attested year, en.wikipedia; no month. The synchronism with the Prague defenestration of May 1618 and with Kircher's October accident is chronological only; no source connects the war to Böhme's resumption.
stops.campa: He begins again, in secret, and does not stop. Within six years he will produce a shelf of books. In May of this year the Bohemian estates throw the emperor's men out of a window at Prague, and the war that follows will run thirty years and burn through Lusatia repeatedly. Görlitz will be occupied, plundered and plagued, its shoemakers and glovers ruined alongside its books. Böhme writes through all of it, and the war does not enter his pages at all, not as siege, not as hunger, not as a single named regiment.
suggested_refs: The Bohemian Revolt of May 1618 and the Lusatian theatre of the Thirty Years' War

stops.name: Görlitz, De Tribus Principiis completed
stops.date_confidence: attested year, en.wikipedia; no month
stops.campa: The second book: De Tribus Principiis, the three principles of the divine being. A dark fiery ground of wrath, a light of love, and the visible world born out of the strife between them. God here is not a serene first cause; God is a will that must have something to work against in order to be anything at all, and evil is not an absence but a real power with a real root. Two centuries on, Schelling will write the Freiheitsschrift out of this dark ground by way of Franz von Baader, and Hegel will call the shoemaker the first German philosopher.
stops.quote: Where Desire is there is also Essence or Being.
stops.quote_source: Jacob Boehme, quoted in Bernard Holland's Introduction to Dialogues on the Supersensual Life, trans. William Law (Project Gutenberg #33742); source treatise unidentified
suggested_refs: De Tribus Principiis (Of the Three Principles of Divine Being), 1619

stops.name: Görlitz, The Threefold Life of Man completed
stops.date_confidence: attested year, en.wikipedia; no month
stops.campa: Vom dreifachen Leben des Menschen: the life in the dark world, the life in the light world, and the outward life of the four elements, all three present at once in one human being who may turn toward any of them. The doctrine has no clergy in it and no sacramental machinery. A man is saved or damned by the direction of his own will, hourly, at the bench or in the street, and the church that holds the keys goes unmentioned. Richter is preaching two hundred metres up the hill.
stops.quote: When thou standest still from the thinking of Self, and the willing of Self.
stops.quote_source: Jacob Boehme, The Dialogues on the Supersensual Life, Dialogue I, trans. William Law (Project Gutenberg #33742)
suggested_refs: Vom dreifachen Leben des Menschen (The Threefold Life of Man), 1620
sources: Dialogues on the Supersensual Life, trans. William Law

stops.name: Görlitz, De Signatura Rerum completed
stops.date_confidence: attested year, en.wikipedia; no month
stops.campa: The signature of all things: every creature, every plant, every metal carries on its outside the mark of the spirit working inside it, and the world is therefore readable by anyone who learns the alphabet. It is a doctrine a shoemaker can hold and a doctor of theology cannot refute, because it asks for no Latin and no license, only attention to what stands in front of you. Paracelsus is behind it, and behind Paracelsus are the dyers' vats and the metalworkers' shops of the Neisse valley.
stops.quote: Therefore, the greatest understanding lies in the signature. For by the external form of all creatures; by their voice and action, as well as by their instigation, inclination, and desire, their hidden spirit is made known.
stops.quote_source: Jacob Boehme, Signatura Rerum, quoted in Alexander Whyte, Jacob Behmen: An Appreciation (1895)
suggested_refs: De Signatura Rerum (The Signature of All Things), 1621
sources: Alexander Whyte, Jacob Behmen: An Appreciation (1895)

stops.name: Görlitz, the circle of noble readers
stops.date_confidence: approximate: the circle of noble readers is attested for the early 1620s, but the Aurora copying by Karl Ender von Sercha belongs to 1612 and is not dated here. No month or day.
stops.campa: A circle forms around him: Silesian and Lusatian noblemen, physicians, a few clergy, Karl Ender von Sercha among them, who copy the manuscripts, pass them house to house and press him to write more. None of it is printed. The books travel as handwriting, through country estates between Görlitz, Liegnitz and Breslau, and they will still be travelling that way in the Netherlands and in England a generation later, when the printers finally get hold of them.
suggested_refs: The manuscript circulation of Böhme's treatises among the Silesian and Lusatian gentry

stops.name: Görlitz, Mysterium Magnum completed
stops.date_confidence: attested year, en.wikipedia; no month
stops.campa: The last great book: a commentary on Genesis running to the length of several ordinary books, taking the whole history from the abyss before creation through Adam, Cain, the flood and the patriarchs, and reading every episode twice, once as history and once as a process inside a soul. He is a merchant of gloves and yarn with no Hebrew. He writes it in about a year, at night, in a town inside a war, and it runs longer than anything else he sets down.
stops.quote: Love is higher than the Highest. Love is greater than the Greatest.
stops.quote_source: Jacob Boehme, The Dialogues on the Supersensual Life, Dialogue I, trans. William Law (Project Gutenberg #33742)
suggested_refs: Mysterium Magnum, the Genesis commentary of 1623
sources: Dialogues on the Supersensual Life, trans. William Law

segments.name: The Way to Christ and the Last Journey

stops.name: Görlitz, Der Weg zu Christo printed without him
stops.date_confidence: disputed and NOT resolved: en.wikipedia gives 1 January 1624, the New World Encyclopedia gives 1623. Both are carried; 1 January 1624 is used for placement.
stops.campa: On New Year's Day a friend puts one of his devotional pieces through a press without his full sanction, and Der Weg zu Christo becomes the only book of his printed while he lives. English Wikipedia dates it to the first of January 1624; the New World Encyclopedia says 1623. It is the gentlest thing he ever wrote, short treatises on repentance and on resignation, with almost none of the alchemy in it. It also finishes him. Richter reads the printed book and begins again.
stops.quote: If thou dost once every hour throw thyself by faith beyond all creatures into the abysmal mercy of God, into the sufferings of Christ, and into the fellowship of His intercession, then thou shalt receive power from above.
stops.quote_source: Jacob Boehme, The Way to Christ, quoted in Alexander Whyte, Jacob Behmen: An Appreciation (1895)
suggested_refs: Der Weg zu Christo, the only work of Böhme's printed in his lifetime

stops.name: Görlitz, summoned before the town council
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by en.wikipedia; the only town council summons in the record
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of March he stands before the town council of Görlitz, the body that made him a citizen twenty-five years before, and is told to leave the town or be driven out. Richter has preached against him again and put a pamphlet into print; the council has the book in front of it and no appetite for being the town that harbours an enthusiast in the sixth year of a religious war. He is forty-eight. His wife and his grown sons are here and the trade that feeds them is here.
suggested_refs: The Görlitz town council summons of 26 March 1624

stops.name: Görlitz, departure for Dresden
stops.date_confidence: attested by en.wikipedia; some accounts give 8 or 9 May. Görlitz pin originated fresh for this journey: a grep across all corpus journey files returned no hits for Görlitz, so nothing could be inherited.
stops.campa: On the eighth of May he leaves Görlitz for Dresden, a hundred kilometres up the Elbe road, and will not see his town again until he comes home to die in it. He goes to the Saxon electoral capital because the men who have read his manuscripts have connections there and because Görlitz is closed. He carries nothing printed. Everything he has written except one small book exists as copies in other men's houses, and he leaves it all behind him in the hands of the circle.
suggested_refs: The Elbe road from Görlitz to Dresden, taken 8 May 1624

stops.name: Dresden, the examination that does not condemn him
stops.date_confidence: arrival May 1624 attested; the two-month stay with an unnamed court physician is attested. Venue refused: no source places either the lodging or the colloquium at the Residenzschloss, and the pool's 'July 1624' for the professors' counsel is arithmetic, not a source date. Dresden pin inherited byte-identical from mikhail_bakunin.journey.json.
stops.campa: Dresden receives him well. He lodges two months with a court physician whose name the sources do not give, and the electoral professors and clergy examine him on his doctrine, decline to condemn him, and advise him to go home to his family. No censure is issued and nothing is required of him. Twelve years earlier his own parish had settled the same question in one sermon, a preacher forbidding him the sacrament over the same writings the capital now lets pass unpunished. The physician's house is unlocated and the room of the colloquium is unnamed.
stops.quote: Thou must hate thy own Will, and forbear from doing that to which thy own Will doth drive thee.
stops.quote_source: Jacob Boehme, The Dialogues on the Supersensual Life, Dialogue I, trans. William Law (Project Gutenberg #33742)
suggested_refs: The Dresden colloquium of 1624, at which the electoral theologians declined to condemn him

stops.name: Silesia, the estate of Herr von Schweinitz
stops.date_confidence: summer 1624 per en.wikipedia; the pool's geography lens gave 'autumn 1624' and 'October-November 1624' without support and is overruled. The estate is unlocated: several Silesian families bore the name and no source identifies the seat. The coordinate is a Lower Silesian placeholder near Legnica, not a documented site.
stops.campa: Invited by a nobleman named von Schweinitz, he goes out to a country seat in Silesia and begins what will be his last work, a hundred and seventy-seven theosophic questions, of which he answers only a fraction. Which Schweinitz, and which house, no source consulted can say. He is the guest of gentry now, the shoemaker who was arrested for writing, and the questions he sets himself in this borrowed room concern the nature of the soul and where it stood before the body was made for it.
suggested_refs: The 177 Theosophic Questions, begun in Silesia in the summer of 1624 and left unfinished

stops.name: The Silesian road, the sick man travels home
stops.date_confidence: date attested by en.wikipedia; the route is undocumented, no waystation is named in any source, and the coordinate is an approximate midpoint rather than a stop.
stops.campa: A bowel complaint takes him at the estate and does not let go; other accounts call it dropsy. On the seventh of November he travels back toward Görlitz, sixty or seventy kilometres of Silesian road in November, a sick man of forty-nine in a cart. No waystation of this journey is recorded and the route drawn here is a reconstruction. The unanswered questions travel home in his baggage. He reaches his own house and is put to bed in it, and the town that ordered him out in March does not stop him at the gate.

stops.name: Görlitz, the examination of a dying man's faith
stops.date_confidence: attested that a Glaubensverhör was held at his bedside before the sacraments were given (en.wikipedia; de.wikipedia); no day is recorded and 15 November is a placeholder inside the final illness.
stops.campa: Before the clergy of Görlitz will bring him the sacrament they hold a formal examination of his faith at his bedside. A dying man of forty-nine, propped up on pillows, is asked whether he holds to the Augsburg Confession, whether he believes in the Trinity, what he means by the eternal nature. He answers to their satisfaction and they give him communion. The sacrament reaches him on the strength of an examination, and the same parish will refuse his body a Christian burial inside the fortnight.
suggested_refs: The deathbed Glaubensverhör of November 1624

stops.name: Görlitz, the death of the shoemaker
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by en.wikipedia, de.wikipedia and the New World Encyclopedia. The last words are traditional, carried by the New World Encyclopedia from a death-bed account, not documentary.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of November, ten days after coming home, he dies in his own house at forty-nine. The traditional death-bed account gives his last words as a single sentence about going into Paradise. He has been a herdboy, an apprentice, a master of the shoemakers' craft with a licensed stall on the Untermarkt, a merchant of gloves and yarn, a defendant twice over, and the author of some thirty books, exactly one of which has been printed while he lived to see it.
stops.quote: Now I go hence, into Paradise.
stops.quote_source: Traditional death-bed account, quoted in the New World Encyclopedia, 'Jakob Böhme'
suggested_refs: The house at the former Prager Straße, Görlitz, where Böhme died on 17 November 1624

stops.name: Görlitz, the parish refuses him burial
stops.date_confidence: attested that Richter's successor initially refused a Christian burial and that the burial was delayed (de.wikipedia); no date is given for the refusal or the funeral, and 18 November is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Gregorius Richter has died earlier the same year and cannot object; his successor in the parish objects instead, and refuses at first to give the body a Christian burial. The family petitions, the matter is settled, and the funeral is held after a delay, with a pastor preaching over him under protest. The whole of Böhme's dealings with his own church, from the denunciation of 1612 to this, take place inside one parish and are conducted by two men in succession holding one office.
suggested_refs: The delayed funeral of November 1624 and the successor pastor's refusal

stops.name: Görlitz, buried at the Nikolaifriedhof
stops.date_confidence: burial in the Nikolaifriedhof attested (de.wikipedia); the day is not recorded and 20 November is a placeholder after the delay. The desecration is stated as fact by de.wikipedia and as tradition by the New World Encyclopedia and by Stoudt and Weeks; no primary account was re-verified, and the two confidence levels are not harmonised here.
stops.campa: He is buried in the Nikolaifriedhof outside the walls by the Nikolaitor, the town's burying ground since the twelfth century. A marker is set over him. Within days a crowd, worked up by what has been preached, defiles it. German Wikipedia states the desecration flatly; the older biographical tradition carries it too, and no primary account of the act was re-verified for this file. A stone labelled Grabmal Jakob Böhme stands in the cemetery today among some eight hundred and fifty surviving stones. Whether it is the one that was defiled, nobody has established.
suggested_refs: The Grabmal Jakob Böhme in the Nikolaifriedhof, Görlitz

stops.name: Amsterdam, the manuscripts gathered and printed
stops.date_confidence: attested year, en.wikipedia; no month. The first complete printed edition follows in 1730, publisher and place unspecified in the source.
stops.campa: Fifty-eight years after his death the manuscripts that travelled from country house to country house are gathered and printed together at Amsterdam, with money and help from the Dutch statesman Coenraad van Beuningen. Richter's own son has by then edited a volume of extracts from the writings his father tried to suppress. A complete edition follows in 1730. Behmenists are already meeting in England and in the Netherlands, and Quakers are carrying the doctrine to America.
suggested_refs: The Amsterdam edition of 1682, assisted by Coenraad van Beuningen

stops.name: London, William Law's edition and the Freher plates
stops.date_confidence: the four-volume English edition appears between 1764 and 1781; 1764 is the start. Blake's remark on the Freher plates is reported without a date in en.wikipedia.
stops.campa: William Law issues Böhme in four English volumes between 1764 and 1781, illustrated with the symbolic engravings Dionysius Andreas Freher had made for the purpose: wheels, eyes, hinged flaps that lift to show the fall of Lucifer underneath. William Blake knows the book and says of the plates that Michelangelo could not have surpassed them. Between 1645 and 1662 nearly the whole corpus had already gone into English, and Morgan Llwyd had put two pamphlets into Welsh for the hill farms of the north.
stops.quote: Michelangelo could not have surpassed them.
stops.quote_source: William Blake on the Freher plates in William Law's edition, reported in English Wikipedia, 'Jacob Boehme'
suggested_refs: William Law's four-volume edition (1764-1781) with the engraved plates of Dionysius Andreas Freher

stops.name: Jena, the book put into the hands of Novalis
stops.date_confidence: summer 1799 per novalis.journey.json, which names Böhme directly; no day. Saint-Martin's German study is undated in de.wikipedia, which says 'fast fünfzigjährig', nearly fifty. Jena pin inherited byte-identical from novalis.journey.json.
stops.campa: Louis Claude de Saint-Martin learns German at nearly fifty in order to read Böhme in the original, and his championing sends the books back across the Rhine to a country that had largely forgotten them. At Jena in the summer of 1799 Ludwig Tieck puts a volume of Böhme into the hands of Novalis, and the blue flower and the mining cosmology of Heinrich von Ofterdingen come out of the reading. Schelling, Baader, Hegel and Schopenhauer are all at him within a decade, a shoemaker's private theology becoming the underground current of an entire generation of German philosophy.

stops.name: Görlitz, the shoemaker seated in bronze
stops.date_confidence: unveiling attested to the day by de.wikipedia. The 1898 site was a small plaza by the Görlitz Stadtbrücke at 51.1503, 15.0009; the statue was moved to the Friedenspark in 1972, and the coordinate here is the Friedenspark, where it now stands. The relocation is carried as reconstruction.
stops.campa: On the thirty-first of October, Reformation Day, Görlitz unveils a bronze seated figure of its shoemaker, cast by the Berlin sculptor Johannes Pfuhl, on a small plaza by the town bridge. The town that arrested him, banned his writing and ordered him out sits him down in bronze two hundred and seventy-four years later. In 1972 the German Democratic Republic, which honours him as a dialectician and a humanist rather than as a mystic, moves the statue into the Park of Peace.

stops.name: Dresden, the thought made walkable
stops.date_confidence: exhibition year attested by de.wikipedia; no month. The Episcopal Church addition is dated 2022 with a feast on 11 May (en.wikipedia); the EKD commemoration falls annually on 17 November.
stops.campa: Dresden, which examined him and let him go in 1624, builds his cosmology as a walkable thought-structure in an exhibition four hundred years afterward. The Evangelical Church in Germany keeps his day on the seventeenth of November, the day he died. In 2022 the Episcopal Church in the United States adds Jacob Boehme to its calendar with a feast on the eleventh of May. Blavatsky's Theosophical Society had already claimed him as an ancestor of theosophia, and Steiner named him a forerunner of spiritual science.
suggested_refs: The 2017 Dresden exhibition presenting Böhme's cosmology as a walkable structure
